newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Soymeal prices seen easing as supply squeeze fades.
newsitem.headline: Soymeal prices seen easing as supply squeeze fades.

text.p: Soymeal prices are seen easing over the next six months after a short-term supply crunch, which sent prices soaring in the first quarter of 1997 is eliminated, oilseeds analysts said on Tuesday.

Record soybean crops in Brazil and Argentina will begin reaching the world market in the second half of 1996. This increased supply combined with reduced consumption in Europe, plus the region's switch to lower-priced feedstuffs, and a slowdown in Chinese buying will help trim prices, the analysts said at a feed ingredients conference in Singapore.
"The prospects for April/September 1997 are for declining soyameal prices," a report by Thomas Mielke, editor of Oil World publications which was made available on Tuesday, said.
James Fry, managing director of LMC International Ltd in Britain, said "most of the (recent) surge has been due to short-term tightness in supplies."
"Notwithstanding strong Asian demand growth, there is little evidence to suggest that prices are likely to deviate from their long-term downward trend," he said.
Dealers around the region said buyers had been complaining recently about steep prices for soymeal.
Prices of U.S. meal coming into Southeast Asia were recently seen touching as high as US$360 a tonne C&F for May/June shipment on a Panamax against a price below $300 in early November.

Mielke said China, whose robust buying has helped underpin prices in the market, will probably reduce its level of imports to 1.34 million tonnes from April to September from 1.48 million tonnes in the same period last year.
"Chinese soymeal imports are likely to fall...due to high domestic stocks and too high world market prices," he said.

But the bearish assessment for soymeal may already be running into trouble due to problems such as prolonged cold and wet weather in North America, which has delayed the start of field work this year, and dry weather in parts of Europe.
"However, it is still early in the year and the key planting and growing period are still ahead," Mielke said.
